CS10-01.note: Passage: seawater dissolved ash, grew interlocking crystals, reaction never finished, material 'required' seawater - A. B inverts (crystals sealed then weakened), C invents a surface layer, D restates the modern-binder property the text assigns to portland concrete, so it is a real misread. passage_needed FALSE on the subject-recall channel: self-healing Roman marine concrete is one of the most widely circulated materials-science stories, and a student who has met it picks A from the options alone. The option set by itself is not decisive; topic recognition is.

CS10-02.note: Waves rework the uppermost couplets in shallow water, so shallow counts are systematically short - B. A inverts the direction (extra couplets in deep water), C blames a counting rule, D blames compaction; each is a mechanism a student could believe and none is decidable without the text, since the passage's own contribution is which direction the bias runs.

CS10-03.note: 'They governed how many pages a number ran, not which characters survived it' - length yes, plot no, i.e. C. A is the exact inversion and is the received view the passage is correcting, which makes it the strongest distractor. B (reprints) and D (timing) are off-axis but plausible. The A/C inversion cannot be resolved from the options; the passage is load-bearing.

CS10-04.note: Final sentence: experienced recruits ignore the dance and return to a remembered patch - C. A is a fair description of the MIDDLE of the passage (the over-water flights) rather than the final sentence, which is the misread the item is built on; it is rejectable only by tracking which sentence is asked about. B and D describe events the passage never reports, so they are weaker.

CS10-05.note: D is a near-verbatim lift of the passage's penultimate sentence ('drain water quickly and let the root zone warm'), which is why this grades easy: a student who finds that sentence is done, no structural reading required. A is the erosion account the passage explicitly says does not predict the gravel, B (rainwater storage) contradicts 'drain quickly', C (frost heave) is unsupported. No second defensible option, but the verbatim match makes this the softest item in the set.

CS10-06.note: The survey clusters short lines by copyist, and the closing sentence names the target: 'A device of the poets would not follow the hands' - so the finding undercuts the critics' speech-marking device, C. D is the item's real trap and I considered flagging it: doubting that short lines cluster in direct-speech passages sounds like the same claim. It is not - the survey sorted by copyist RATHER than by passage, so it measured nothing about where in the poem the lines fall; it rebuts authorial origin, not passage distribution. A inverts the conclusion's target onto the editors. Hard: the answer is the argumentative target of a one-clause conclusion.

CS10-07.note: CONFIRMING the elimination stage on option A: A is backwards twice over. The passage says on overcast nights city and country read within half a degree, and as physics the nocturnal UHI is suppressed under cloud and wind because it is built by radiative cooling of the rural site under a clear sky. A student who knows any of this rejects A with the passage covered, which is what makes the distractor set weak. B (rural station siting) is off-topic; C is the only near miss - the passage does open on the daily mean diluting the signal - but the text supplies no daytime data at all, so 'concentrated after sunset' is not established by it and the closing sentences point at weather type, not time of day. Not defensible enough to flag. passage_needed FALSE: 'calm, clear nights' is the textbook answer, so subject recall reaches D unaided.

CS10-08.note: Names/genealogies travel in oral transmission, procedural detail does not; 'the genealogies may be inherited, but the quarrels were composed' - B. The four options are a clean permutation of inherit/compose over genealogies/disputes/formulas, so every distractor is one swap away and none is rejectable on shape. This is the best-built option set in the batch.

CS10-09.note: 'The color curve, and not the total energy released, is what identified the debris' - the rate of reddening, D. B is the option the passage explicitly rules out in the same sentence, which makes it a strong trap for a student who reads only the last clause; C re-offers the nickel expectation as the answer; A invents a delay. Some recall risk (the 2017 kilonova lanthanide-opacity story is public), but the discriminating detail - reddening rate vs total energy - is specific enough that I judge the passage genuinely required.

CS10-10.note: Travel required a cash deposit and a landowning guarantor; destitution kept people off the road - migrants came from households with the means, C. D ('spare a worker once sowing was done') is a genuinely attractive real-world account of seasonal labor that the passage never offers; A overshoots to the top of the distribution when the text says the middle; B invents a chain-migration mechanism. Every distractor maps to a misreading a real student makes.

CS10-11.note: Text 2 is entirely about a dumbbell pupil spreading wavelengths to different focal depths - B, stated outright. The distractors are excellent because each is a REAL color mechanism from another taxon (A layered retina, C colored oil droplets in birds, D the mantis shrimp's scanning eye), so a knowledgeable student cannot reject them as biology. But passage_needed is FALSE on the recall channel: the chromatic-blur hypothesis for cephalopod color vision was widely covered, and 'colorblind octopus solves color by refocusing through a weird pupil' is retrievable as a unit. Easy because Text 2 states the mechanism in its first clause.

CS10-12.note: Sealed instruments deposited with the town council = terms recorded elsewhere with a third party, A. C (private ledgers) and D (unwritten custom) are decent misreads of 'recorded elsewhere' and of the silence itself; B (word of mouth) is close to the Text 1 position the response is rebutting, so it is the weakest. Easy: A is a paraphrase of Text 2's second sentence.

CS10-13.note: Text 2 names growth and fecundity costs and says slow growers lose space on storm-scoured reefs - A. B (reversion when the warm season ends) and C (less carbon translocated to the host) are both real, documented costs of heat-tolerant symbionts, so a student with subject knowledge cannot eliminate them; only Text 2 says WHICH cost is being pressed. That is exactly the right way to build a cross-text item - domain knowledge makes the distractors harder, not the key easier.

CS10-14.note: Text 2 is a fire-lighting argument: lowers ignition temperature, treated tinder caught where untreated stayed cold - D. A is the nearest miss and stays in the fire frame (heat retention rather than ignition); B restates the pigment reading being rebutted; C is unsupported. passage_needed FALSE on recall: the manganese-dioxide-as-fire-making finding for Neanderthal sites is a well-publicised result, and it is retrievable from the stem's subject alone.

CS10-16.note: Text 2: where one substrate dominated the creole reproduces that substrate's marker order; the universal template surfaces only 'where the inherited options conflict' - i.e. where substrates disagreed, A. B is the precise inversion and is the item's whole difficulty; C and D substitute a survival-of-the-substrate axis that neither text raises. Hard because the key requires converting 'many substrates mixed' into 'the inherited options disagreed' - an inference the text supports without stating in those terms.

CS10-17.note: Text 2's first sentence: ratios record elevation AND distance travelled inland - C. A (amount of rainfall) and B (temperature) are both genuinely true of oxygen isotope ratios in precipitation - the amount effect and the temperature effect are standard - so this is the good case where real knowledge makes the distractors MORE attractive while only Text 2 fixes which factor is being pressed. Easy only because Text 2 names it in the opening line; a strong set.

CS10-18.note: Text 2: the emblem books belonged to a narrow clerical readership while the pictures hung in dining rooms and were priced by the square foot - the readerships do not overlap, D. C is the best distractor because it keeps the access argument but shifts it onto painters rather than buyers, which is the wrong party; A (language) and B (engravings not mottoes) are inventions. Easy: D paraphrases Text 2's middle sentence.
